analysis.one_liner: Bans doctors from referring Medicare patients to clinics or suppliers they own or profit from.
analysis.headline: The House Ways and Means Committee approved the ban on Medicare self-referrals in June 1989, but the bill never got a House floor vote before the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for a doctor to send a Medicare patient to a lab, imaging center, dialysis clinic, or other facility in which the doctor, or an immediate family member, holds a financial stake or receives payment. Entities would have been barred from billing Medicare for services supplied on such a referral, with fines of up to $15,000 per improper claim and $100,000 per scheme to dodge the ban. The goal was to take the financial incentive out of medical referrals so patients get ordered only the care they need. The committee approved it, but it never reached the House floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare patients, who would get referrals driven by medical need rather than by their doctor's investments, and taxpayers, who fund Medicare and would no longer pay for services ordered to feed a doctor's ownership stake.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits a physician (or immediate family member) from referring a Medicare patient to an entity the physician has an ownership or investment interest in, or receives compensation from.
Bars the entity from presenting a Medicare claim, or billing the patient or any other payer, for services furnished under a prohibited referral.

Subjects anyone who bills for services they know or should know are prohibited to a civil fine of up to $15,000 per service, and anyone who builds a circumvention scheme, such as cross-referral deals, to a fine of up to $100,000 per scheme.
Requires anyone who collected money for prohibited services to refund it, and denies Medicare payment for such services outright.

Carves out protections against abuse of the ban's loopholes by requiring HHS to write regulations defining indirect ownership and what counts as the sole rural provider, within six months of enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Physicians and their families who own stakes in labs, imaging centers, dialysis units, medical equipment suppliers, and similar Medicare businesses, which would lose a referral pipeline, plus the entities themselves.

drawbacks.text: The ban is riddled with exceptions: publicly traded securities, hospitals, ambulatory surgical centers, in-office ancillary services, rural sole providers, and various rental, employment, and recruitment arrangements are all excluded, which limits how much self-referral it actually stops.
Financial relationships already legally binding before February 9, 1989 get a one-year grace period before the ban applies to their referrals.

Compliance would be complex: doctors, group practices, and hospitals would have to untangle ownership, leases, and compensation arrangements, and HHS would face a six-month deadline to write major regulations, an administrative burden honest providers would bear alongside bad actors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is a strong consumer protection: removing the incentive for doctors to order profitable services. The main honest objections are compliance complexity for legitimate practices and the long list of exceptions that would let some self-dealing continue. On balance the public benefit outweighs the cost, and the exception list was the price of drafting a workable ban.

outcome.mechanism: The House subcommittee and full committee approved the bill and ordered it reported in June 1989, but no report was issued, no floor vote was ever scheduled, and the 101st Congress ended with it dead.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark introduced the Ethics in Patient Referrals Act of 1989 on February 9, 1989, with five original cosponsors.
It was referred to both the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees, then to their health subcommittees, which held hearings on March 2 and June 1, 1989.
On June 13, 1989 the health subcommittee amended the bill and forwarded it to the full Ways and Means Committee, which marked it up and ordered it reported on June 29, 1989.
No further action appears in the record: the bill was never reported to the House and never received a floor vote before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
The bill had 21 cosponsors, 20 House Democrats and 1 House Republican, and won committee approval, but that was not enough to get it to the floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Physicians and entities holding ownership stakes in Medicare-serving facilities kept their self-referral arrangements legal for the rest of the Congress; Medicare patients went another session without this protection.

industries.industry: Physician-owned labs, imaging centers, and dialysis clinics
industries.note: The bill would cut off Medicare business built on their owners' own referrals. That revenue comes from patients ordered to facilities their doctors profit from, so the industry's interest runs against patient care and Medicare costs.

The bill bans outside self-referral but explicitly permits in-office ancillary services billed by the physician's own group practice, locking in the doctor's role as both referrer and provider for in-office care.

With physician-owned competitors barred from capturing referrals, patients flow back to independent hospitals, which are also allowed to keep compensating doctors for recruitment and services at fair market value under defined exceptions.
Ownership in exchange-listed companies with over $100 million in assets is expressly excluded from the ban, so large corporate providers can keep physician investors and the referrals they bring.
